co_river_wall_ii.blurb: A small cliff just beneath the Buttonrock reservoir dam in the St. Vrain canyons outside Lyons. About two dozen lines mix bolted sport and gear routes, and the terrain ranges from delicate slab to steep, pumpy faces and strenuous cracks. Most of the grades sit between 5.11 and 5.14, with only a couple of easier lines, including a short 5.8 slab that works as a footwork-focused warm-up. Several lines can be rigged for top-rope. The river breeze can keep the base cool, while the wall may bake when the sun is on it, so early or late in the day is kinder on hot afternoons.

co_turkey_perch.blurb: A single-pitch granite crag in the Turkey Rocks cluster of the South Platte, near Woodland Park. Nearly everything here is traditional protection: hand and fist cracks, chimneys and offwidths, with the bulk of the grades from 5.6 to 5.9 and just a few harder lines up to 5.12. Good rock and a friendly spread make it a sensible choice for newer trad leaders, and many lines can be set up for top-rope. The standout line is Steppenwolf, an offwidth with a hidden hold. Expect solid jamming rather than face climbing, and note that older ratings in this region tend to feel stiff.

co_dog_house_the.blurb: A steep, heavily overhung sport crag beside Tunnel 5 in Clear Creek Canyon, west of Golden. Routes are roughly 60 to 80 feet and favor power and stamina. Most bolted lines fall in the 5.11 to 5.12 range, with a few 5.10s and a handful at the top of the scale, plus a few boulder problems and a couple of top-rope options. Many lines carry playful dog-themed names. A flat area at the base makes belaying easy, though the hillside up to it is steep and prickly. Newer climbs may still carry a little loose rock, and some grades are still being settled.

co_crimpfest_wall_the.blurb: A steep-to-vertical wall in the Devil's Head part of the South Platte, split by roofs and corners. Nearly all of the two dozen or so lines are bolted sport routes, with a pair of gear lines, and they run long, around 100 feet, so bring a 60 m rope. Climbing is thin, technical and crimpy rather than juggy. Almost everything is 5.11 or 5.12, so it suits strong leaders, with only a stray easier route on the far end. Lines begin in a shaded gully on the left and spread rightward for about 200 feet. Flaky, high quality stone makes for sustained, rewarding pitches.

co_outer_gates.blurb: The southern fringe of the Monastery crags above Big Thompson Canyon near Estes Park. All of the roughly two dozen routes are bolted, and the stone is steep-to-slabby granitic pegmatite with good friction and plenty of features, so the challenge is often choosing holds. Most lines are moderate, from the 5.7s to 5.10 with one at 5.11, making this one of the friendlier and busier corners of the Monastery. Climbs cluster tightly around the Steeple, Vestry and Wine Cellar. Expect a long, steep hike in and out, and cooler conditions on cloudy days.

co_country_club_cave.blurb: The big central cave of the Golf Wall, a steep limestone cliff of sport routes north of Durango. This is where the hard lines live: two dozen or so pumpy, overhanging climbs of about 40 to 50 feet, almost all 5.11 to 5.13 with a few warm-ups beside the cave. Fixed chain draws are common, which makes for quick laps. Easier routes belong on the cliff's left end instead. Spring and fall are the prime seasons, though winter and summer can work if you pick sun or shade to suit the day.
